lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Application or project: appointment preparation and questions

objective: Learners prepare a real list of questions and information for one real upcoming appointment (such as a medical, dental, school, or counseling appointment) and review that list with a trusted adult before the appointment takes place.
scenario: With a trusted adult, the learner identifies one real upcoming appointment, thinks through what information the appointment will likely require and what questions they want answered, writes a complete list, and reviews it with the trusted adult before the appointment happens; the adult confirms the review took place.
safetyNotes: The learner does not attend or conduct the appointment as part of this lesson; only preparation and review with a trusted adult are required.
No real outside party (the appointment provider) is contacted as part of this task; only the learner's own list and a household review are required.
Completing this task sheet never certifies the review by itself; a guardian confirmation is required before the task counts as complete.

simulationAlternative.description: If the learner has no real upcoming appointment, they instead choose a realistic fictional appointment scenario (such as a first dental visit or a school counselor meeting) and role-play the full preparation and question-review conversation with a trusted adult, with the adult asking follow-up questions the way an appointment provider might, for the same level of review and feedback.

materials: paper or a document to write the question list
information about the real upcoming appointment (date, type, provider) if one exists, or a chosen fictional scenario

tasks.directions: Think about a real upcoming appointment you have, or if you don't have one, pick a realistic fictional scenario.

prompts.text: Name the appointment type (real or fictional) and what you already know about what it's for.

tasks.directions: Think through what information you'll likely need to provide and what questions you want to ask.

prompts.text: I listed at least three pieces of information I might be asked to provide (such as my age, the reason for the visit, or relevant history).
I wrote at least three specific questions I want answered during the appointment.
Write your full list of information and questions in the order you'd want to bring them up.

tasks.directions: Review your full list with a trusted adult before the appointment, or for a fictional scenario, role-play the conversation together.

prompts.text: Did you review your list with a trusted adult?
choices: Yes, I reviewed it before a real appointment
Yes, I role-played it for a fictional scenario

prompts.text: Write down one thing your trusted adult added or changed on your list during the review.

tasks.directions: Think about how the review changed your list.

prompts.text: Explain one question or piece of information you hadn't thought of before your trusted adult reviewed your list, and why it matters.

remediation: If a learner's questions are too vague to get a useful answer at the appointment (such as 'is everything okay?'), reteach by having them rewrite each vague question into a specific one naming exactly what they want to know (for example, changing 'is everything okay?' to 'what should I do if this symptom comes back?'), before returning to the full review with their adult.
extension: Have the learner prepare a second, shorter version of their list meant for a situation where they only have two minutes to ask their most important question, and explain which question they kept and why.
